name: Backpressure
intent: When a consumer cannot keep up, push that fact back to the producer so it slows down, instead of letting work pile up until something breaks.
scenario: A service reads events from a sensor feed at 20 per second and writes them to a database that can take 8 per second. The in-memory buffer between them grows, delays grow with it, and eventually the process runs out of memory and crashes, losing everything in the buffer.
problem: Whenever a producer is faster than a consumer, the difference has to go somewhere. An unbounded queue just hides the problem: memory grows, latency grows (old data is processed long after it mattered), and the failure arrives later and bigger. Some part of the system must be told to slow down or let go.

howItWorks.title: Notice the mismatch
howItWorks.text: Measure queue depth, the age of the oldest item, and the time work spends waiting. A queue that only ever grows means the consumer is slower than the producer on average, and no buffer will fix that.

howItWorks.title: Bound every buffer
howItWorks.text: Every queue, channel and in-memory list gets a maximum size. A bound turns an invisible, slowly growing problem into an explicit decision about what to do when the buffer is full.

howItWorks.title: Choice 1: slow the producer down
howItWorks.text: Block the producer, make it wait, or have the consumer ask for items at its own pace (pull, or credit-based flow control such as reactive streams and TCP windows). Nothing is lost, and the whole pipeline runs at the speed of its slowest part.

howItWorks.title: Choice 2: shed load
howItWorks.text: If delay is worse than loss, drop items when full: drop the newest, drop the oldest, or sample. Reject with an error such as HTTP 503 or 429 so callers can back off. This suits metrics, telemetry and live video, not payments.

howItWorks.title: Choice 3: add capacity, deliberately
howItWorks.text: Scaling consumers can help with sustained load, but it is slow to take effect and has a limit, so it must be combined with bounds and a policy. Propagate the signal upstream across every hop, because one unbounded stage can hide the problem again.

pros: Keeps memory and latency bounded and predictable
Turns overload into a controlled, visible decision
Protects the slowest part of the system from being overwhelmed
Failure is gradual (slower or lossy) rather than a sudden crash
cons: Slowing producers pushes the problem to whoever feeds them
Dropping data is only acceptable for some kinds of data
Needs support in every stage, or one unbounded stage defeats it
Hard to tune: too small a buffer wastes throughput on bursts
whenToUse: Pipelines where a fast stage feeds a slow one
Streaming and event processing, queue consumers, request handlers with thread pools
Any service that could be overloaded by its callers
whenNotToUse: A producer that is always slower than its consumer (nothing to push back)
Where the producer genuinely cannot slow down and data cannot be lost: add capacity or durable storage instead
pitfalls: Unbounded queues anywhere in the path, including thread pool task queues and in-memory buffers
Dropping silently with no metric, so data loss is invisible
Applying backpressure at one hop while the next hop buffers without limit
Retrying rejected work immediately, which adds load to a system that asked for less

roles.label: Producer
roles.description: Generates work and should slow down when told to.

roles.label: Bounded buffer
roles.description: Holds a limited amount of work and signals when it is full.

roles.label: Consumer
roles.description: Processes work at its own limited speed.

quiz.question: A log pipeline has a fast collector feeding a slow indexer through an in-memory queue with no size limit. After a traffic surge, the collector process runs out of memory and dies hours later. What is the best first change?
options: Bound the queue and decide what the collector does when it is full
Give the collector more memory so that it can survive for a longer time under load
Add a second unbounded queue after the indexer to take the overflow from the first
Speed up the collector so that it clears the surge of events a lot sooner
quiz.explanation: An unbounded buffer only delays the failure and makes it bigger. A bound forces an explicit choice: slow down, shed or scale. More memory just postpones the crash.

quiz.question: A payments service writes charges to a queue consumed by a slower ledger service. The queue is full. The team must decide between dropping the newest charges and making the payments service wait. Which is the sound choice?
options: Drop the oldest charges from the queue, since the newer ones are more relevant
Make the producer wait or reject with 503, since losing a charge is worse than delay
Drop charges at random so that the average delay stays low for the remaining ones
Buffer in memory beyond the limit until the ledger service has caught up again
quiz.explanation: Shedding suits data like telemetry, not money. For payments the signal must slow the producer, with an error the caller can retry later. Extra buffering just reintroduces the unbounded queue.

quiz.question: A service returns 503 when its queue is full. Clients retry immediately in a loop, and the queue never drains, though the service had a short blip only. What should the clients do?
options: Retry faster so that at least some of the requests manage to get through
Open more connections so that the retries are spread across the servers evenly
Back off with a growing, jittered delay and respect Retry-After
Retry only one time after exactly one second, the same for every client
quiz.explanation: An immediate retry adds load to a system that asked for less. Growing, randomised delays let it recover, and a fixed one-second retry makes all clients arrive in lockstep.
